newsitem.title: USA: Criminal charges possible in tainted berries case.
newsitem.headline: Criminal charges possible in tainted berries case.

text.p: The company that distributed tainted strawberries making 150 schoolchildren ill and exposing 9,000 other students to the hepatitis-A virus, could face criminal charges, officials said on Wednesday.
"It looks like the products were grown in Mexico, which means the company was in violation of the law," a U.S. Department of Agriculture official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said.
Under the law companies must certify in writing that the products they sell to the goverment school lunch programme are grown in the United States.
The Agriculture Department's Office of Inspector General has launched a probe into the matter, department sources said.

The tainted berries were sold to the Agriculture Department as part of its school lunch programme by the San Diego firm of Andrew & Williamson, a processor and packer of foods, which also distributed the fruit to school districts around the country in the form of fruit cups.
The firm's parent company, Epitope Inc., based in Beaverton, Ore., announced on Wednesday that A&W would recall 13 lots of strawberries that were shipped in early December 1996.

"The health and well-being of the public is A&W's foremost concern," Epitope Chief Executive Adolph Ferro said. "While it is not certain that the lots being recalled are contaminated, we want to eliminate all possible risk to consumers."
He said customers were notified and the company was cooperating with the Centres for Disease Control and the Food and Drug Administration.
Epitope, based in Beaverton, Ore., said its subsidiary inaccurately described some of the strawberries associated with the outbreak as having been grown and processed in the United States.

"We have notified the USDA of our concern with regard to this matter and have today accepted the resignation of Fred L. Williamson, the president and chief executive officer of A&W," said Adolph J. Ferro, president and chief executive officer of Epitope. "As the health and well-being of the public remains our foremost concern, we will continue to work with appropriate governmental agencies."
About 150 students and teachers in central and southwest Michigan were confirmed to have contracted the hepatitis A virus after eating the frozen sliced strawberries.
Officials said 28 Michigan counties received the frozen strawberries, which originated from Mexico and were first shipped to the state Dec. 9, 1996.

Dr. David Johnson, chief medical executive of the Michigan Department of Community Health, said health agencies throughout the state have given thousands of injections of immune globulin, which is not a vaccine but contains antibodies, to help prevent the illness.
"It's quite clear that the contamination did not appear at any particular school building. It occurred somewhere upstream," Johnson said.
On Tuesday, public health officials in Los Angeles announced that 9,000 students and school workers may have been exposed to hepatitis-A by eating frozen strawberries from the same tainted batch.

Schools in four other states; Illinois, Florida, Tennessee and Iowa also received frozen strawberries from that batch. A&W shipped strawberries to 17 states but only six received berries from the tainted batch, USDA officials said.
Health officials in Los Angeles were preparing on Wednesday to offer inoculations to the 9,000 students at 18 elementary, middle and high schools who may have been exposed to the virus.

"It's not a panic situation," stressed Dr. Shirley Fannin, the Los Angeles County director of infectious diseases. She added that hepatitis-A has an incubation period of 14 days and the strawberries were consumed last week.
"We're here within a week of consumption. We have another week to plan," she said.
In Chicago, school officials said they did not believe that any of the cases of strawberries shipped to schools there had been consumed, but were still checking.
They said that out of the 1,320 cases sent to Chicago from the California supplier, 971 were still in warehouses and there were no known cases of hepatitis among Chicago students.
Hepatitis-A is easily spread through uncooked food and typically causes a mild liver infection. Symptoms include fatigue, vomiting, abdominal discomfort and jaundice.
The drug immune globulin has proved to be effective in preventing the disease if administered within 14 days of consumption of tainted food.
Shares of Epitope fell sharply on news of the tainted berries, dropping $1.875 to $8.25 on Nasdaq.
